content: The mathematical model Policy1-Cervix was utilized to estimate the risks associated with key cervical cancer screening and treatment strategies in 78 lowand middle-income countries. A separate model was applied to assess outcomes specifically for women living with HIV in Tanzania, focusing on cervical cancer incidence, mortality, precancer treatment, and potential preterm deliveries resulting from such treatments. These outcomes were evaluated over the lifetime of birth cohorts eligible for screening starting in 2030. Women and girls aged 15 years and older, regardless of their prior cervical cancer screening or treatment history, were invited to participate in an anonymous, voluntary survey. This survey was promoted through the Union for International Cancer Control, WHO advisory groups for women living with HIV, and WHO regional focal points for cervical cancer elimination initiatives. The WHO recommends using HPV DNA testing as the primary screening method for women living with HIV, rather than visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) or cytology. This recommendation is based on moderate-certainty evidence and is conditional. For women who test positive for HPV DNA, triage methods such as partial genotyping, colposcopy, VIA, or cytology are suggested, with the choice depending on feasibility, training, program quality assurance, and available resources. Regular cervical cancer screening is recommended to begin at age 25 for women living with HIV, as evidence suggests that cervical cancer is rare in women younger than 25. Screening can be discontinued after age 50 if two consecutive negative results are obtained, consistent with recommended screening intervals. VIA and ablation treatments are not suitable for women whose cervical transformation zone is not visible. Priority should be given to screening women living with HIV aged 25–49 years. A screening interval of every 3–5 years is suggested when using HPV DNA testing as the primary method. In settings where HPV DNA testing is not yet available, existing programs using cytology or VIA should continue until HPV DNA testing becomes operational. For women with histologically confirmed adenocarcinoma in situ, WHO recommends large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) or cold-knife conization. LLETZ may be preferred for women of reproductive age, while cold-knife conization may be chosen when precise margin interpretation of the histological specimen is critical. HPV vaccines should be introduced as part of a coordinated strategy to prevent cervical cancer, targeting girls aged 9–14 years before they become sexually active. A three-dose schedule is recommended for those aged 15 years and older, as well as for immunocompromised individuals, including those living with HIV. For cardiovascular disease prevention in people living with HIV, strategies addressing modifiable risk factors such as blood pressure, smoking, obesity, unhealthy diet, and physical inactivity should be implemented. Chronic HIV care provides an opportunity to integrate interventions like nutrition assessment, dietary counseling, smoking cessation, exercise promotion, and blood pressure monitoring to reduce the risk of noncommunicable diseases and improve HIV treatment outcomes. People living with HIV have an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases compared to HIV-negative individuals. This risk is influenced by chronic immune activation, inflammation, and traditional cardiovascular risk factors. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) has been associated with both benefits and risks for cardiovascular health. While some antiretroviral drugs, such as protease inhibitors, may contribute to lipid abnormalities and increased cardiovascular risk, the overall benefits of ART in reducing HIV-related morbidity and mortality outweigh these risks. Cardiovascular disease screening is recommended for people living with HIV, as studies have shown a 40–70% higher risk of myocardial infarction and cerebrovascular disease in this population compared to HIV-negative controls. Chronic immune activation and inflammation, even with suppressed viral loads, contribute to this increased risk. Integrating cardiovascular risk management into HIV care is essential to address this growing health concern.
